A vision at Corinth: “Be not afraid, but speak” Acts 18:9–10
At night in Jerusalem: “so must thou bear witness also at Rome” Acts 23:11
His own list of sufferings 2 Corinthians 11:23–27

One square for each chapter of the books that name Paul: 182 verses in 44 chapters. The darker the square, the more verses in it name him. Choose a chapter to read what happens there.
And Paul, earnestly beholding the council, said, Men and brethren, I have lived in all good conscience before God until this day.
A Pharisee, son of a Pharisee
At night in Jerusalem: “so must thou bear witness also at Rome”
No verse in Matthew, Mark, Luke or John names him.
Born at Tarsus, brought up in Jerusalem
But Paul said, I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city: and, I beseech thee, suffer me to speak unto the people.
Born a Jew in Tarsus in Cilicia, “a citizen of no mean city”, and “brought up in this city” (Jerusalem) “at the feet of Gamaliel”.
And cast him out of the city, and stoned him: and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man’s feet, whose name was Saul.
A “young man … whose name was Saul” kept the clothes of those who stoned Stephen, and “was consenting unto his death”.
And desired of him letters to Damascus to the synagogues, that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem.
He “made havock of the church”, putting men and women in prison, and asked the high priest for letters to bring believers bound from Damascus.
And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?
Then the disciples took him by night, and let him down by the wall in a basket.
After his conversion he preached in the synagogues of Damascus, went into Arabia, came back to Damascus, and escaped over the wall in a basket.
CHAPTER III · THE CHURCH IN ACTS
Three journeys, arrest, Rome; the letters · 14 records
¶ So they, being sent forth by the Holy Ghost, departed unto Seleucia; and from thence they sailed to Cyprus.
First journey: sent out from Antioch with Barnabas to Cyprus and the cities of Pisidia and Lycaonia; at Lystra he was stoned and left for dead.
Antioch in Syria, Salamis, Paphos, Perga, Antioch in Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe
And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.

He parted from Barnabas over Mark and set out with Silas. Timothy joined them at Lystra; a vision called them to Macedonia; they went on to Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea and Athens, and he stayed eighteen months at Corinth.
Barnabas, Silas (Silvanus), Timothy, John Mark, Aquila, Priscilla and 1 more
Lystra, Troas, Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Athens, Corinth
And when neither sun nor stars in many days appeared, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope that we should be saved was then taken away.
On the voyage to Rome the ship was wrecked at Melita (Malta). At Rome he lived two whole years in his own hired house with a soldier guarding him, receiving all who came.
And when we came to Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard: but Paul was suffered to dwell by himself with a soldier that kept him.
Prisons named in Scripture: Philippi, where he and Silas were put in the stocks; Herod's judgment hall at Caesarea; and Rome. In several letters he writes as a prisoner.
The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.

The letters to Timothy and Titus name journeys that are hard to place in Acts: Timothy left at Ephesus when Paul went into Macedonia, Titus left in Crete, a winter planned at Nicopolis, a cloak left at Troas and Trophimus left sick at Miletum.
Tradition, by who said it and when · 6 sources
What Scripture says of his end

Acts ends with Paul two whole years in his own hired house in Rome, “Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him.”

In 2 Timothy he writes as a prisoner in Rome who has already made his “first answer” in court: “the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith”.
Whether Paul wrote 2 Timothy is debated, as the Letters page shows; Scripture does not record his death.

VIEWS, WITH WHO HOLDS THEM · THIS PAGE
Did the men with Saul hear the voice? Acts 9:7 says they were “hearing a voice”; Acts 22:9 that “they heard not the voice of him that spake to me”. (In date order.)
They heard a sound, not the words
Matthew Henry (early 18th century); W. J. Conybeare and J. S. Howson (1891), who also report Wordsworth and Hackett
Henry: they heard “a confused noise” but did not understand what was said. Conybeare and Howson: the voice spoke articulately to Saul, but to the rest it was “a sound mysterious and indistinct”.
Scholars Acts 9:7·Acts 22:9 Matthew Henry, 1706-1721·W. J. Conybeare and J. S. Howson, 1891
Leave the differences as they stand
W. J. Conybeare and J. S. Howson (1891)

They judge it “both more prudent and more honest to leave these well-known discrepancies exactly as they are found in the Bible”, and note that readers explain them differently according to their view of inspiration.
